title: I got tired of crypto trading bots, so I built an analysis-first alternative
author: Every-Cheesecake-856
selftext:
I’ve spent a lot of time looking at crypto trading bots from the perspective of both a developer and someone who actually cares about risk, and I think the “does this bot make money?” question is slightly backwards.

A bot is not an edge.

If the underlying strategy is bad, automating it just makes you lose money faster. And a backtest or a screenshot of a profitable trade tells you very little about how something behaves through different market regimes, slippage, liquidity changes and ugly volatility.

That’s actually why I built CryptoYaanBot .com.

I didn’t want to build another black-box bot that says LONG/SHORT and asks you to trust it. I wanted something closer to a lightweight trading desk that helps me do the analysis and, more importantly, forces me to think about risk before the trade.

The workflow is basically:

• Give it any coin and timeframe and it analyzes market structure and trend across multiple timeframes.

• It identifies support/resistance, momentum, RSI, volume, order blocks and fair value gaps.

• It checks the market across Binance, Bybit, Mexc and OKX rather than blindly trusting one exchange.

• It produces a 0–100 setup score and actually shows the factors contributing to that score.

• If there is a setup, it gives an entry area, invalidation/stop and multiple targets with R-based levels.

• Position sizing is calculated around your account size and risk tolerance instead of just throwing out a random entry.

• For futures, it also checks leverage and approximate liquidation against the stop, which is something I think many traders completely underestimate.

• There is a scanner that ranks setups instead of making you manually check 50 charts.

• There are live volume alerts that can lead you into a full analysis rather than simply shouting “BUY.”

• You can ask questions conversationally, like “Is ETH overbought?”, “Compare BTC and SOL”, or “Are there any decent 4h setups?”

• There’s also a market overview, P&L/profit calculator and scheduled market scans.

The important part is that I deliberately did NOT make it an auto-trading bot.

The AI is there to explain the analysis, not invent numbers or pretend it can predict the future. The idea is to give you the data, reasoning, setup and downside first, then let you make the decision.

For example, instead of:

“BTC LONG 🚀 95% WIN RATE”

you get something closer to:

“Here is the current trend. Here are the important levels. Here is why the setup scored 83/100. Here is the entry area. Here is where the thesis is invalidated. Here is the potential reward relative to the risk. Here is what the other exchanges are showing.”

That distinction matters to me.

I’m not claiming CryptoYaanBot .com magically makes anyone profitable. I don’t think any honest developer can promise that. Markets change, strategies fail and sometimes the best trade is no trade.

What I’m trying to solve is the other problem: traders making decisions from 15 different charts, indicators, Telegram messages and emotions, while barely thinking about position size or invalidation.

If you want to try it, the basic analysis is free and you don't need to connect a wallet or exchange account.

I'd actually be interested in criticism from people here who build systematic strategies or algo-trading systems. Especially around the scoring methodology, risk model and what you'd want to see added before trusting an analysis engine.

I'm much more interested in making the analysis better than convincing anyone that a bot can print money.

comments.author: ozgqr
comments.body: The 0–100 score seems most valuable if it is calibrated by market regime rather than treated as a universal confidence number. I’d separate trend, liquidity, volatility and setup-quality components, then show how each performed out of sample across trending, ranging and high-volatility periods. That would make the explanation more useful than simply adding more indicators, and gives Marx a clearer way to represent uncertainty in an agent’s decision context.

replies.author: Every-Cheesecake-856
replies.body:
Agreed on all of it, and the regime point is the one I keep coming back to. Right now the score is built from separate components already: trend, momentum, location against key levels, multi-timeframe agreement, so I can at least say why a given number came out the way it did. What it does not do yet is the part you are describing: weight those components differently depending on whether the market is trending, ranging, or whippy, and report how each has actually held up out of sample in each state. A 55 in a clean trend and a 55 in chop are not the same thing, and treating the number as one universal confidence reading hides that.

Splitting the backtest by regime is the honest version of this, and it is harder than it sounds, mostly because labeling the regime after the fact is trivial and doing it in real time without hindsight is not. But you are right that it beats bolting on more indicators, which usually adds correlation, not information.

On the uncertainty point, that is where I think this should end up: the score carrying a confidence band that widens in regimes where that setup type has been unreliable, instead of a bare number. Curious how you have handled regime labeling without leaking future data, that is the part I keep getting stuck on.
